title: Walter Page and the walking bass
summary: Page, a teacher and baritone player, pioneered the high walking bass line that led to five-string basses.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Well, Walter Page, though, he was a very good musician.
Oh, yeah. He was a music teacher at the University of Kansas. Sure, he was a baritone player, fantastic baritone player.
Well, what did he -- I mean, just apart from playing the bass in there, what did he contribute to the

He contributed that -- I don't know what note it is on the bass but when the band would be swinging and nothing but the rhythm section would be -- you know, the whole band would lay out and they would call it the strolling bass, the walking bass, you know. He would go way up, (Humming) and come right on down. And he started that. And he started with four strings. And the bass players, after they started hearing it, they couldn't get that high on the bass so they started making a five string bass with that extra string on it so they could sound like Walter Page, you know. I think Chubby Jackson was the first one to start playing that five string, it was a Kay bass, they put the fifth string on it. And that would enable you to bing, bing.

Because he went way beyond the keyboard of the bass, whatever that is. He'd go almost down to the sound post, you know, bing, bing, bing (humming). You know. Oh, man. And when the band would start doing that, oh, man. It used to send chills up me every night when I'd hear the rhythm section. The whole band would be shouting, you know. And we'd get to like the middle part, the bridge, and all of a sudden it would just -- everybody would drop out but the rhythm section (humming). Oh, my goodness.
That's the greatest band ever been on earth -- swinging. I've never heard a band swing like that. Oh, God, it's --
